## A repository is not a journal

The previous section explains why a repository is a natural container for mathematical work whose artifacts evolve asynchronously. It does not follow that a repository can replace the institutions that traditionally determine which mathematical claims deserve durable scholarly status.

A software repository is optimized for preservation, modification, executable artifacts, collaboration, and change history. A journal historically performs a different set of epistemic functions: it organizes peer scrutiny, evaluates novelty, filters significance, establishes a stable citation object, records responsibility, and participates in the long-term canonicalization of the result. These functions overlap, but they are not interchangeable.

A public repository can establish that a manuscript existed at a particular time. It can preserve every revision and associate formal source files with a paper. It can make computational certificates reproducible. It can expose changes that a conventional publication workflow might hide behind replacement PDFs. None of this determines whether a theorem is new, important, correctly attributed, or adequately understood.

Conversely, traditional journal publication was never a perfect correctness oracle. Referees can miss errors, peer review can be slow, and the published article normally contains no machine-executable certificate from which logical validity can be reconstructed mechanically. The point is therefore not to oppose an infallible journal to an unreliable repository. The two infrastructures provide different kinds of assurance.

Machine-generated mathematics makes those assurances separable enough that they should probably be represented explicitly. A future mathematical object might independently acquire certifications corresponding to formal correctness, semantic correspondence between the formal and informal statements, novelty, attribution, adequacy of exposition, and mathematical significance. One institution need not certify all of them, and they need not mature simultaneously.

This decomposition helps explain why the OpenAI release should be interpreted neither as ordinary preprint publication nor as a substitute for peer review. The repository publishes the evidence package early and makes its evolution observable. The mathematical community must still determine what the package ultimately means.

That distinction is particularly important when hundreds of results arrive at once. Under paper-scale publication, verification effort is largely internalized by authors, collaborators, referees, seminar audiences, and specialists who choose to engage with a particular result. Under result abundance, a laboratory can release a corpus whose aggregate checking cost is much larger than the cost borne by any one outside reader. Open publication is valuable, but it does not by itself solve the allocation problem created when the producer can generate candidate mathematics faster than the external community can review it.

The resulting scholarly system will therefore require both **versionable research objects** and institutions capable of certifying their different epistemic dimensions. Repository semantics solve the first problem. They make the second more visible.

## Versioned evidence, not versioned truth

The most important conceptual distinction in repository mathematics is between the theorem and the changing state of evidence surrounding it.

Let \(T\) denote a mathematical proposition. Its truth value does not change because a repository receives a new commit. What can change at time \(t\) is the dossier through which the mathematical community relates to \(T\). A useful conceptual representation is

$$
D_t(T)=
\bigl(
S_t,
P_t,
F_t,
C_t,
N_t,
R_t,
U_t
\bigr),
$$ {#eq-when-mathematics-became-a-repository-epistemic-dossier}

where \(S_t\) is the current statement of the claim, \(P_t\) the available informal proof material, \(F_t\) the formalization state, \(C_t\) the computational or formal certificates, \(N_t\) the evidence concerning novelty and attribution, \(R_t\) the state of independent review, and \(U_t\) the available human understanding or explanatory reconstruction. The tuple is not intended as a numerical metric. It is a reminder that the epistemic object has several coordinates.

A revision can alter one coordinate without altering the others. Correcting a citation may change \(N_t\) while leaving the proof untouched. Adding a Lean proof can change \(F_t\) and \(C_t\) without changing the natural-language statement. A specialist may later discover a simpler explanation, changing \(U_t\) even though neither the theorem nor its formal certificate changes. A formalization may expose an unstated hypothesis, requiring a revision of \(S_t\) while the formal derivation remains perfectly valid for the proposition it actually encodes.

This is why the phrase *versioned mathematics* is potentially misleading. Mathematical truth is not versioned. **Evidence, representation, provenance, and understanding are.**

The distinction also blocks an inappropriate linear model of verification. It is tempting to imagine a simple progression from unverified manuscript to human-checked theorem to formal proof to established fact. In practice, the states form something closer to a partial order. A classical theorem may be deeply understood and universally accepted without any formal proof. A newly generated theorem may have an impeccable kernel-checked derivation but almost no conceptual exposition. A result can be formally valid yet fail a novelty review. Another can be unquestionably novel while its proof remains under scrutiny.

Repository mathematics therefore requires the state itself to remain inspectable. A single Boolean such as

```yaml id="7npyqv"
verified: true
```

throws away exactly the distinctions that become important under machine-scale publication.

The same applies to corrections. A revision that repairs exposition is different from one that weakens the theorem, adds a hypothesis, changes an attribution, or replaces a failed proof. Ordinary version control records textual difference. Mathematical infrastructure should eventually be able to represent the **semantic type of the revision**.

This is not bureaucratic decoration. Downstream consequences depend on it. If a proof changes while the theorem remains identical, dependent work may need no reassessment. If the theorem itself weakens, every consequence that relied on the stronger statement may have to be revisited. Version history becomes mathematically useful only when the system knows what kind of state changed.

## Lean, Comparator, and the executable layer of the release

Formal proof is the strongest technical mechanism in the OpenAI release for separating proof generation from proof checking. In a system such as Lean, an untrusted producer can generate a large proof object while the trusted kernel checks whether that object establishes the encoded theorem from the accepted definitions and axioms. This changes the verification economics because the computational cost of checking can be dramatically smaller and more reliable than reconstructing the entire argument manually.

But formal verification solves only a precisely delimited problem.

Suppose the informal theorem intended by the paper is \(T_I\), while the proposition encoded in Lean is \(T_F\). A successful formal proof establishes derivability of \(T_F\) in the formal environment. It does not, by itself, establish that

\[
T_I
\]

and

\[
T_F
\]

express the same mathematical claim. The correspondence between the human theorem and the formal theorem is therefore a separate trust boundary.

This is the **semantic specification problem**. It becomes particularly important when the proof itself is machine-generated, because a system could in principle prove a subtly weakened or altered proposition while the accompanying prose encourages readers to interpret it as the original problem. The danger need not involve intentional gaming; ordinary mistakes in formalization are sufficient.

OpenAI's Comparator mechanism addresses one part of this problem by separating the trusted challenge statement from the untrusted solution. Rather than allowing the solution artifact to define freely what counts as success, Comparator checks that the theorem exposed by the solution matches a separately supplied target and that the result satisfies the permitted formal environment.[^when-mathematics-became-a-repository-comparator] The architecture therefore reduces the amount of the generator that must be trusted.

It does not eliminate the final semantic question. Someone still has to determine whether the trusted target itself faithfully represents the theorem mathematicians care about. The complete chain is closer to

\[
T_I
\longleftrightarrow
T_F
\longrightarrow
\text{formal proof}
\longrightarrow
\text{kernel acceptance},
\]

where the first relation requires mathematical interpretation and the latter relations admit increasingly mechanical checking.

This distinction clarifies what formal verification changes. It does not abolish error; it **moves the error surface**. When kernel checking is strong, residual risk shifts toward theorem specification, definitions, axiom policy, provenance, novelty, and interpretation.

That is already visible in the release. Family 003 carefully specifies which zero-free statements are included in the Lean development and which later applications are outside scope. Family 102 exposes several separate hardness statements rather than one vague “UGC formalized” flag. Family 107 explicitly states the arithmetic complexity model formalized by Lean. Family 287 shows that even when the proof artifact exists, metadata describing the formalization can temporarily lag behind it.

Formal proof also clarifies the dual function of mathematical proof itself. A proof is both a **certificate** and an **explanation**. The certificate function answers whether the conclusion follows from the assumptions. The explanatory function identifies the mechanism worth understanding, teaches the reader why the theorem is true, and exposes ideas that may transfer to other problems.

Proof assistants are exceptionally well suited to the first function. They do not automatically supply the second.

This suggests that machine-generated mathematics will increasingly be published as what might be called **proof-carrying mathematics**: a human-readable statement accompanied by a formal statement, one or more proof artifacts, verification configuration, and provenance metadata. The natural-language paper remains necessary because the certificate does not tell the reader which conceptual move matters.

The long-term significance is larger than individual formalizations. Once formal statements, dependencies, and proof objects become machine-readable, a research system can operate over the literature as an executable environment. The loop can become recursive: a model proposes a theorem, another process formalizes it, the kernel verifies it, the result becomes available to later machine reasoning, and new research builds on the now-certified object. Formalization is then no longer an archival afterthought. It is part of the computational substrate of future discovery.

## The production function: from roughly 4,000 problems to 372 result families

The release invites a simple calculation:

\[
\frac{372}{4000}\approx 9.3\%.
\]

It would be tempting to interpret this as a model success rate on frontier mathematics. That interpretation would be unjustified.

The numerator is not a count of independently sampled successes under a fixed protocol. It is the number of released **result families**, some containing several manuscripts and some connected to broader research trajectories. The denominator is approximately 4,000 posed research problems, but the public material does not establish that those problems form a representative sample of a well-defined population. Their difficulty distribution, field distribution, selection mechanism, stopping rules, and degree of overlap are not sufficiently specified for the ratio to estimate a general mathematical capability probability.

Selection after the research runs creates an additional problem. The released corpus is, by definition, the subset judged worth publishing. Failures, partial results, rediscoveries, uninteresting proofs, weak claims, and abandoned trajectories are not represented symmetrically. Any direct success-rate estimate would therefore suffer from severe selection bias.

Nor is the compute allocation homogeneous. OpenAI reports an average roughly equivalent to three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking per released result under the dominant procedure, but averages over selected successes do not reveal how compute was distributed across all attempts. A few expensive trajectories could coexist with many short ones. Some problems may have been retried. Some results were produced outside the dominant fixed procedure. Without the full denominator-level telemetry, a meaningful cost-to-discovery curve cannot be reconstructed.

The right conclusion is therefore not probabilistic but organizational. OpenAI has demonstrated a **research production function** capable of taking a large portfolio of problems as input and emitting hundreds of release-worthy mathematical outputs.

Conceptually, the production system depends on several variables:

\[
R = f(M,C,O,Q,V,H),
\]

where \(M\) denotes model capability, \(C\) available compute, \(O\) the surrounding orchestration and tooling, \(Q\) problem selection, \(V\) verification infrastructure, and \(H\) human intervention or curation. This is not an empirically estimated production equation; it is a decomposition of the factors that have to be separated before any general capability claim can be made.

The important change from earlier demonstrations is that performance is now being expressed at the **portfolio level**. The relevant scientific questions become: which classes of problem benefit most; how discovery probability changes with inference compute; whether formalization alters the selection process; how many results share a common technique; how often failures are recognizable internally; and whether a research system can learn from its own previously generated mathematics.

OpenAI's programme also illustrates a broader shift in AI evaluation. When conventional mathematical benchmarks saturate, evaluation moves toward unsolved research problems. But once a model succeeds on such a problem, the benchmark item ceases to be open. Evaluation itself begins to **consume the frontier**.

That makes open problems an unusual benchmark resource. They are not infinitely reusable test cases. They are pieces of scientific uncertainty that can disappear when solved. As model capability rises, the boundary between evaluation and research therefore dissolves: measuring the system can itself produce new mathematics.

## Selection effects, base rates, and what the release does not establish

The production-function view makes several negative conclusions just as important as the positive ones.

First, the corpus does not tell us how a frontier model performs on a randomly selected unsolved problem. Mathematics has no obvious probability distribution over “all open problems,” and even within one discipline, problem formulations differ radically in maturity, available literature, tractability, and evidential structure. Any global success percentage would conceal more than it revealed.

Second, the release does not establish that the model can autonomously recognize the most important unsolved questions. The problem portfolio was assembled from a human mathematical world in which researchers had already identified conjectures, developed terminology, produced partial results, and estimated significance. The model received highly compressed objects representing decades of human mathematical judgment.

Third, publication is itself a filter. A generated argument that merely reproves known mathematics can be mathematically correct without contributing a new result. A surprising theorem may be excluded if its proof remains too uncertain. A family with several related outputs can contribute one catalogue entry while a single manuscript elsewhere contributes another. Result-family count is therefore neither theorem count nor independent-trial count.

Fourth, the release says little by itself about the relative importance of failures. A system could fail on almost every arbitrary research question while still be scientifically transformative if the minority it solves includes highly consequential bottlenecks. Conversely, a high nominal success rate concentrated on technically accessible but conceptually marginal problems would be less significant than the percentage suggests.

The correct unit is therefore **epistemic throughput**, not raw hit rate. A research system creates value when generated results are valid, genuinely new, mathematically significant, and sufficiently interpretable or formalized to become usable by future research.

Those dimensions are multiplicative in the practical sense that severe failure on any one can destroy most of the value of the output. An invalid theorem has little mathematical value no matter how surprising it is. A correct rediscovery contributes less than a genuinely new result. A correct and novel theorem may remain operationally weak if nobody can understand or reuse it. A major theorem that never becomes visible outside an inaccessible proprietary system contributes little to the shared mathematical corpus.

This is why the October release should be neither dismissed because not every result is independently assimilated nor treated as 372 equally confirmed breakthroughs. It is a heterogeneous corpus produced by a new research mechanism. The scientific task is to characterize the mechanism without erasing the heterogeneity.

## From proof abundance to result abundance

The earlier concept of **proof abundance** described a world in which generating candidate proofs becomes substantially cheaper. The October release suggests a more consequential threshold: **result abundance**, where the rate of apparently significant new mathematical results begins to rise enough that the research community must manage them as a stream.

The distinction matters because proofs and results are not equivalent. A proof settles a proposition. A result becomes part of mathematics only after questions of statement, correctness, novelty, importance, attribution, explanation, and relation to surrounding theory have been sufficiently resolved.

A high-throughput system can therefore create a large amount of *mathematical work* without immediately creating an equal amount of *mathematical knowledge*. The gap between those quantities is the central epistemological problem of result abundance.

Let \(G(t)\) denote the cumulative stock of sufficiently significant generated results by time \(t\), and let \(A(t)\) denote the subset that has been sufficiently assimilated for mathematicians to use them as stable components of further reasoning. Define the conceptual backlog

$$
B(t)=G(t)-A(t).
$$ {#eq-when-mathematics-became-a-repository-epistemic-backlog}

This is not intended as a directly measurable quantity without further operational definitions. Its purpose is to identify a possible regime change. If the rate of significant result generation persistently exceeds the rate of assimilation, then \(B(t)\) grows.

Mathematics has always contained an assimilation lag. Major proofs can take years to simplify and understand. Large classification projects, difficult geometric arguments, and computer-assisted proofs have all required substantial post-publication digestion. The novelty would be **scale**. One notoriously difficult theorem can mobilize a specialist community. Hundreds of difficult results arriving together create an allocation problem.

The emerging object is therefore neither a false theorem nor an unknown theorem. It is an **unmetabolized theorem**: a result with enough evidence to deserve serious attention but whose mechanism, relation to existing theory, consequences, or canonical formulation have not yet been fully absorbed.

This state is not a defect. It is a natural consequence of asynchronous epistemic production. But if it becomes common, mathematics needs institutions designed to reduce the backlog.

## The new bottleneck: mathematical digestion at corpus scale

The operation required after result generation can be called **mathematical digestion**. It includes several distinct activities that conventional research often performs informally and in parallel: triaging which claims deserve urgent attention; validating proofs and formal statements; determining novelty; locating the result inside the existing dependency network; extracting the central idea; identifying reusable methods; deriving downstream consequences; and eventually deciding which formulation deserves to become canonical.

These operations are conceptually different enough that they should not be collapsed into “review.”

A referee can determine that a proof is correct without discovering its most reusable idea. A formalizer can certify the logical structure without establishing whether the argument is historically new. A specialist can understand the proof but fail to see an unexpected application in another field. A survey author can perform the conceptual compression that makes the theorem accessible years after its original publication.

Conceptual compression is particularly important. Let \(P\) denote a complete proof. The mathematical culture rarely retains \(P\) in all of its original detail. It searches for a more compact mechanism \(C(P)\): the smallest intelligible conceptual structure from which the essential proof can be reconstructed by a competent reader. This is not ordinary text summarization. A shorter description can omit the very move that makes the theorem reusable. Good compression preserves the mechanism.

The same applies at corpus scale. Hundreds of manuscripts may contain only a much smaller number of genuinely new methods. If ten results rely on variants of one underlying construction, then treating them as ten unrelated successes obscures the scientifically important fact. Mathematical digestion should therefore include **conceptual deduplication**: identifying when apparently distinct outputs share the same reusable idea.

The dependency network adds another dimension. A new theorem can convert previously conditional statements into unconditional ones, eliminate hypotheses, provide new lemmas for unrelated fields, or invalidate a research direction based on an assumed obstruction. The effect of a theorem is therefore not fully captured by its own statement. It is the change induced in the graph of mathematical consequences.

A mature digestion pipeline would consequently ask not only:

> Is this result correct?

but also:

> What does this result make newly possible?

That question can expose an **epistemic delta** much larger than the original paper.

Canonicalization is the final stage. Mathematics survives partly by forgetting. Fields cannot retain every proof detail, historical detour, computational trace, or failed approach at equal prominence. They compress the durable contribution into named theorems, standard definitions, reusable lemmas, canonical constructions, and textbook arguments.

Result abundance therefore makes canonicalization more, not less, important. Storage is cheap. Human conceptual memory is scarce.

The situation also changes what an “AI mathematician” should mean. A single model that generates proofs is only one component of the research system. At scale, a more realistic architecture resembles an **AI mathematical organization** composed of distinct functions: discoverer, critic, formalizer, literature analyst, verifier, expositor, method extractor, and curator. Humans may participate at every stage.

The decisive criterion of digestion is not that somebody has read the original manuscript. A result has been genuinely assimilated when future mathematical reasoning can exploit it without repeatedly reconstructing the entire original proof. At that point, the theorem has become part of the working substrate of the discipline.

## Authorship, responsibility, and mathematics without a human knower

Result abundance also breaks apart assumptions that the traditional author line usually keeps bundled.

In conventional mathematical work, authorship often implies several things simultaneously. The authors contributed substantially to the result, understand the proof, stand behind its correctness, chose how it should be presented, and accept scholarly responsibility for the publication. These functions are not philosophically identical, but ordinary research practice lets one name perform them all.

Machine-generated mathematics separates them.

An AI system can generate a proof that no individual human could reproduce immediately. A formal verifier can provide strong logical assurance without possessing human understanding at all. A researcher can later write the explanation that makes the result comprehensible while having contributed nothing to the original discovery. An institution can decide to release the work and assume responsibility for the publication even though no named employee authored the inferential steps in the conventional sense.

OpenAI's repository already reflects this partially through institutional authorship and explicit computational provenance. The relevant questions therefore become more granular:

\[
Q:\text{Who formulated or selected the question?}
\]

\[
G:\text{Who or what generated the result?}
\]

\[
V:\text{Who or what verified it?}
\]

\[
E:\text{Who produced the exposition?}
\]

\[
R:\text{Who accepts responsibility for releasing it?}
\]

These roles may be occupied by different humans, models, tools, and institutions.

The distinction matters because **causal contribution is not the same as epistemic responsibility**. A proof assistant can contribute decisive assurance to the correctness of a formal derivation, but it cannot assume responsibility for an overstated press claim. A model can generate the central argument, but it cannot resolve a priority dispute through scholarly judgment. An institution can decide to publish a corpus even when no individual within it has reconstructed every proof.

This makes provenance necessary but insufficient. A complete provenance chain might record the problem source, prompt or task construction, model and version, inference procedure, intermediate reasoning artifacts where retained, manuscript generation, formal statement, formal proof, human edits, and independent reviews. Such a chain tells us how the result came to exist. It does not itself tell us who should answer if the release misstates novelty, omits prior work, or presents an uncertain result as established.

Responsibility therefore has to remain attached to persons or institutions capable of exercising judgment.

Credit is likely to fragment in parallel. Future mathematical priority disputes may distinguish **problem priority**, **method priority**, **proof priority**, **formalization priority**, and **expository priority**. This is not entirely new; mathematics already distinguishes conjecturers, solvers, simplifiers, and generalizers. AI makes the decomposition harder to avoid because generation and understanding can occur in different places and at different times.

Prior literature attribution becomes particularly important. A model can rediscover a result or technique without direct access during the inference episode to the exact paper in which the idea first appeared. Independent rediscovery may be intellectually real while still failing to constitute novelty. Automated generation therefore increases rather than decreases the need for careful literature comparison.

The deepest change concerns the relation between authorship and understanding. A theorem may become institutionally possessed before it is individually possessed: the laboratory can hold a manuscript, a formal certificate, computational artifacts, and provenance sufficient to justify release even though no single human can yet explain the whole argument in the way expected of a traditional author.

That possibility motivates the distinction between **generator** and **epistemic guarantor**. A future human author or responsible editor may not have originated every inferential step but may be expected to reconstruct the theorem sufficiently to defend its statement, explain the essential mechanism, validate the correspondence between formal and informal versions, and accept responsibility for its scholarly presentation.

Such a role would preserve a meaningful human responsibility layer without pretending that humans generated mathematics they did not generate.

The point is not to reserve authorship for humans by definition, nor to deny that future systems may acquire increasingly sophisticated mathematical agency. It is to avoid the opposite mistake: treating automation of mathematical contribution as automation of scholarly accountability.

The October release therefore forces an uncomfortable but productive separation. A mathematical statement can be generated by a machine, formally certified by another computational process, released under an institution's name, and only later become fully understood by individual mathematicians. Once those events are temporally and organizationally distinct, authorship can no longer function as the sole summary of how mathematical knowledge came to exist.

[^when-mathematics-became-a-repository-comparator]: OpenAI. (2026). **Math research repository: formal verification and Comparator artifacts**. _GitHub_. The repository includes Comparator challenge material used to separate trusted target statements from untrusted generated solutions for selected formalized results. [Repository](https://github.com/openai/math).

## The AGMAI intervention and the governance of machine-generated mathematics

The release did not occur in an institutional vacuum. By late September 2026, a group of senior mathematicians had formed the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence (AGMAI) after OpenAI had approached some of them about a possible external advisory body. AGMAI chose to organize independently, with no decision-making authority inside the company and no claim to represent it. Its membership included François Charles, Camillo De Lellis, Timothy Gowers, Martin Hairer, Nikhil Srivastava, Ulrike Tillmann, Ravi Vakil, Edward Witten, and Melanie Matchett Wood.[^when-mathematics-became-a-repository-agmai-formation]

AGMAI's 29 September recommendations were based on more than 600 community responses and articulated three principles that are directly relevant to the October release. First, significant AI-generated mathematical results should be released responsibly and promptly. Second, laboratories releasing substantial mathematical output that is not yet fully understood by humans should support—financially as well as technically—the subsequent development of human understanding. Third, the direction of that understanding should remain organically determined by the mathematical community rather than by the laboratory that produced the results.[^when-mathematics-became-a-repository-agmai-recommendations]

The recommendations also went further upstream. AGMAI asked laboratories to stop testing advanced mathematical problems on proprietary models that were unavailable to the broader scientific community. The concern was not merely that researchers might learn about results late. It was that a two-tier research system could emerge in which a small number of organizations control models and compute capable of attacking public mathematical problems before the community itself has comparable access.

That concern is structurally different from ordinary disputes over publication timing. Open mathematical problems are non-rival intellectual objects: one mathematician's knowledge of a conjecture does not prevent another from working on it. Frontier inference, by contrast, is scarce and allocatable. If only a few institutions possess enough model capability and compute to pursue thousands of open problems at once, equal formal permission to work on mathematics no longer implies equal effective opportunity to do so.

The resulting asymmetry can be described as a transfer from a public commons to a privately controlled research layer. The literature is public, the conjectures are public, and the historical partial results are public; the frontier model and the compute budget may not be. Publishing the final theorem restores access to the output but does not restore equality of opportunity in the discovery process.

This is why downstream publication rules, although necessary, cannot by themselves solve the governance problem. The most consequential decisions may occur earlier: which models are accessible, who receives inference budgets, which problems are selected, how much compute each receives, which successes are amplified, and which generated results receive follow-up formalization or exposition.

In practice, governance spans several layers. Model training determines what capability exists. Access rules determine who can use it. Problem selection determines where capability is deployed. Compute allocation determines how intensively each direction is pursued. Release policy determines what enters the public record. Formalization and exposition determine which outputs become easy to trust and understand. Funding for subsequent mathematical digestion determines which results receive sustained attention.

The farther upstream the decision, the less ordinary publication reform can compensate for it later.

This makes AGMAI's recommendation to stop frontier testing on inaccessible proprietary models more significant than a generic call for openness. It asserts that responsible release after the fact is insufficient if the research opportunity itself was distributed inequitably.

There is a legitimate counterargument. If a private laboratory possesses a model capable of resolving an important open problem, refusing to use that capability until equal access exists may delay knowledge that could otherwise become public. The governance problem therefore contains a real trade-off among scientific knowledge production, equity of access, preservation of human research agency, and the norms through which priority and understanding are created. None can simply be maximized without affecting the others.

The dispute became concrete in public reporting around the October release. Wired reported that OpenAI had convened roughly forty mathematicians in August to discuss how mathematical research should be handled if AI systems began to outrun ordinary human research throughput. According to the report, participants including Bryna Kra urged the company not to release results primarily through tweets, blog posts, or undigested mass publication, but to provide papers that mathematicians could understand and build upon. Some attendees believed that OpenAI had indicated it would not release everything simultaneously; OpenAI said it was unaware of having made that commitment.[^when-mathematics-became-a-repository-wired-mathematicians]

The final October release partly reflects those concerns. It includes full manuscripts, formalization work, provenance, version history, reasoning summaries for selected cases, and an explicit commitment to support workshops, conferences, and programmes aimed at understanding major AI-generated results. At the same time, it remains a mass release outside the conventional publication process, and the generating model itself was not publicly available at the time of publication.

The same Wired report discussed a separate and contested dispute involving Tristan Buckmaster and collaborators' Navier--Stokes work. Buckmaster alleged that OpenAI devoted substantial resources to a nearby problem after learning that his group was making progress, and he raised concerns about priority, authorship, and interactions he interpreted as coercive. OpenAI and Sébastien Bubeck disputed material parts of that characterization. Buckmaster also publicly stated that he did not know whether OpenAI had used his group's data and was not accusing the company of doing so.[^when-mathematics-became-a-repository-wired-mathematicians] The episode should therefore not be treated as established misconduct. Its relevance here is institutional: once frontier-scale AI research can be rapidly redirected toward a problem, compute asymmetry can affect priority even before any theorem is published.

NYU's Courant Institute separately described the smooth-forcing blow-up work by Buckmaster and collaborators as a significant advance toward the Navier--Stokes problem, developed from earlier work by Diego Córdoba and Luis Martínez-Zoroa and involving both language-model assistance and Lean verification.[^when-mathematics-became-a-repository-nyu-navier-stokes] The combination of human research, AI assistance, formal verification, and priority sensitivity illustrates why governance debates are likely to intensify as machine research becomes more capable.

AGMAI's 6 October statement therefore described the OpenAI release not as the completion of a mathematical process but as its beginning. Participation by individual mathematicians in discussions with laboratories, it stressed, should not be interpreted as endorsement of every subsequent release decision. More substantively, the statement argued that mathematicians must retain the capacity to formulate their own questions, pursue their own approaches, and explore directions not selected by AI laboratories; equitable access to powerful tools and sufficient compute was presented as a condition of that freedom.[^when-mathematics-became-a-repository-agmai-october]

The governance problem can consequently be expressed as a question of **epistemic separation of powers**. The institution that generates frontier mathematics should not automatically be the sole archive, verifier, interpreter, allocator of attention, funder of understanding, and arbiter of significance. Even when every individual function is competently performed, concentrating all of them in one actor creates correlated incentives and correlated failure modes.

The appropriate response is not to deny private laboratories a role. They may remain the organizations best able to build the strongest research systems. The problem is whether mathematical knowledge and mathematical agency can remain plural once those systems become major producers of the frontier.

## When the scarce resource becomes mathematical agency

The previous sections traced several migrations of scarcity. As candidate proofs become cheaper, verification becomes relatively more valuable. As formal verification scales, conceptual understanding becomes relatively scarcer. As significant results arrive in portfolios, method extraction, attention, and canonicalization become harder.

The more fundamental transition occurs further upstream. Once computational research capacity becomes abundant enough, the scarce resource is not merely the ability to attack a problem. It is **the authority and capacity to decide which problems are attacked**.

That is mathematical agency.

In this article, *mathematical agency* means the capacity to choose, formulate, and pursue a research direction rather than merely to solve a supplied theorem. The distinction matters because mathematical research begins before proof search. Someone must decide what is worth asking.

An established open problem is already a compressed product of mathematical judgment. Before a conjecture becomes a recognized target, researchers have normally determined that the observed pattern is nontrivial, that the formulation captures something important, that the hypotheses are meaningful, that the problem interacts productively with surrounding theory, and that enough partial evidence exists to justify sustained effort.

A model evaluated on famous open problems therefore receives much of this upstream work for free. The frontier has already been mapped.

This suggests a distinction between **frontier solving** and **frontier construction**. Frontier solving asks whether a system can make decisive progress on an important unresolved question. Frontier construction asks whether the system can identify which unresolved questions should become important in the first place.

The latter requires more than search. It includes noticing phenomena that deserve explanation, inventing useful definitions, recognizing connections between fields, deciding which assumptions should be weakened, detecting anomalies that deserve to become conjectures, and judging whether a technically accessible problem is mathematically fertile.

These activities are often grouped under the elusive term *mathematical taste*.

The October programme provides unusually strong evidence about machine discovery on human-selected problems. It provides much less evidence about autonomous question formation and question selection. Yet as proof generation becomes more capable, those upstream functions become more valuable rather than less.

The resource-allocation problem makes the point concrete. Suppose a research system can investigate only a finite subset of a much larger space of plausible mathematical questions. Then every allocation of inference to one problem rather than another expresses a judgment about expected value, tractability, prestige, scientific importance, strategic relevance, or demonstration value. At low throughput this may resemble ordinary experimental design. At high throughput it becomes agenda setting.

AI compute therefore begins to resemble research funding, but with a more direct effect. A funding body allocates money to researchers, who retain substantial autonomy over how they pursue the work. A laboratory operating a mathematical AI system can allocate machine cognition directly to a problem, expand successful trajectories, terminate unproductive ones, or redirect thousands of inference runs rapidly. The research agenda becomes partially programmable.

This is why better theorem generation increases the value of mathematical taste. If solution capability is weak, problem selection matters but many selected questions will remain unresolved. If solution capability becomes strong across a broad portfolio, then a marginal improvement in deciding what deserves attention can have multiplicative effects.

A system that proves famous conjectures is therefore not automatically equivalent to one that can create mathematics of comparable long-run depth. Famous conjectures have already passed through decades of human selection. A deeper test would ask whether the system can identify tomorrow's important conjectures before mathematicians have named them.

Definitions provide an even stronger test. Many of the most consequential episodes in mathematical history were not simply proofs of difficult pre-existing propositions. They introduced concepts that changed which questions could be asked at all. A powerful definition can reorganize several fields simultaneously by revealing that apparently different phenomena instantiate the same structure.

Advanced mathematical agency must therefore include the ability to generate not only proofs but useful questions, definitions, invariants, methods, and theories.

The governance implications follow directly. If frontier systems merely accelerated calculations requested by mathematicians, unequal access would resemble an infrastructure problem familiar from other sciences. If they can resolve substantial parts of the open frontier and eventually help determine which questions populate the next frontier, access becomes a question of **agenda-setting power**.

The critical inequality is then not merely unequal tool access. It is unequal capacity to determine what receives frontier-scale mathematical cognition.

This can occur even without philosophically autonomous AI. The immediate agent may be the institution. A laboratory has goals, budgets, product incentives, evaluation targets, compute-allocation policies, and release strategies. The model itself need not possess an independent agenda for the laboratory to exercise substantial mathematical agency through it.

This distinction avoids an unproductive reduction of the debate to whether AI systems “really want” anything. Institutional agency is already sufficient to shape the frontier.

The possible future is not necessarily zero-sum. Widely accessible research systems could substantially increase individual human agency. A mathematician might explore ten speculative ideas where today only one is affordable; a graduate student could test conjectures before investing years in them; researchers at small institutions could summon literature search, formalization, proof exploration, and computational assistance previously available only through large collaborations.

In that architecture, AI becomes an agency multiplier.

The opposite architecture is also possible: a few laboratories select the major questions, allocate the strongest systems, publish the resulting frontier, and leave the wider community primarily to verify, explain, and metabolize the output. Human mathematicians remain intellectually active, but agenda sovereignty moves upstream into the organizations controlling machine cognition.

These are different institutional futures built from the same underlying technology.

A useful hierarchy therefore distinguishes at least four forms of agency. The weakest is choosing among supplied problems. A stronger form is formulating new questions within an existing theory. Stronger again is inventing concepts and methods that create new problem spaces. The broadest is shaping the priorities of a mathematical community.

The October release primarily demonstrates what can happen when powerful systems are deployed on the first of these levels at substantial scale. The harder scientific questions concern the second and third. The governance debate concerns the fourth.

The central scarcity in a mature high-throughput regime may therefore become the right to decide **what is worth knowing before the answer exists**.

## Who controls the frontier?

Once mathematical agency becomes an allocatable computational resource, the institutional question can no longer be reduced to whether model weights are open.

Effective research capability depends on a stack: model capability, inference compute, research orchestration, formal and computational tools, access rules, and governance of the research programme. Open weights without sufficient compute may decentralize little. Public compute without access to sufficiently capable models may do the same. A proprietary model with broad, affordable research access could in some circumstances distribute more effective agency than nominally open weights that only a handful of institutions can run at frontier scale.

The relevant object is therefore the **research infrastructure**, not the license alone.

Several institutional architectures are already visible. The first is the private frontier laboratory: the same organization controls the model, compute, problem selection, research workflow, and release process. Its advantage is speed. The organization can modify the research stack quickly, allocate large amounts of inference without interinstitutional negotiation, and integrate model development with experimentation. The October corpus demonstrates how productive such an arrangement can be.

Its weakness is the concentration of capability and agenda. Researchers outside the laboratory observe selected outputs more readily than the full distribution of attempted questions, compute allocation, negative results, and internal selection decisions. The architecture is optimized for throughput, not necessarily for distributed mathematical agency.

A second architecture retains private model ownership while expanding researcher access. OpenAI's *ChatGPT for Academic Researchers* programme, announced in July 2026, stated an ambition to provide free frontier-model access to 100,000 scientists, mathematicians, and engineers through 2027. OpenAI said that its initial programme had been planned for 10,000 researchers and that, after receiving more than 13,000 applications representing as many as 65,000 requested seats, eligible first-wave applicants would be selected by lottery.[^when-mathematics-became-a-repository-openai-academic-access]

This changes the agency equation substantially because the researcher, rather than the laboratory, can select the problem. But provider-mediated access is not identical to infrastructure control. The provider still determines which models are exposed, usage limits, tool access, policy constraints, continuity, and eligibility. Access to generally available frontier models should also not be conflated with access to the exact internal model that generated the October mathematics corpus. OpenAI's mathematics announcement separately said that the company was working toward a responsible release of that model.[^when-mathematics-became-a-repository-openai-release]

A third architecture treats AI capability as public scientific infrastructure. The U.S. National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource (NAIRR) is an early example. NSF describes it as national infrastructure connecting researchers to compute, models, data, software, and expertise; by October 2026, NSF reported support for more than 600 research projects and 6,000 students.[^when-mathematics-became-a-repository-nairr] NSF also announced a $100 million State and Regional AI Infrastructure Hubs programme intended to broaden access to AI compute and resources.[^when-mathematics-became-a-repository-nairr-hubs]

The institutional significance is that access governance becomes at least partially separable from ownership of any one model. The infrastructure can allocate resources according to scientific criteria rather than exclusively according to the commercial provider's product strategy.

Europe is pursuing a related strategy at larger sovereign-compute scale. By April 2026, the European Commission reported nineteen AI Factories deployed across European supercomputing infrastructure, with further regional access points, while the AI Gigafactory initiative aimed to expand capacity and explicitly included academic access among its objectives.[^when-mathematics-became-a-repository-eu-ai-infrastructure] These programmes are not mathematics-specific, but if high-end inference becomes a scientific instrument, they provide a plausible institutional basis for allocating machine cognition as shared research infrastructure.

The analogy with telescopes and particle accelerators is useful but incomplete. Astronomers compete for observation time; physicists share expensive experimental facilities. AI research systems differ because the instrument increasingly overlaps with the intellectual role of the researcher. It does not merely observe a phenomenon. It can propose lemmas, select approaches, generate proofs, formalize them, and perhaps eventually choose subsequent questions.

That makes governance of the instrument unusually consequential.

@tbl-when-mathematics-became-a-repository-control-architectures summarizes the principal trade-offs without pretending that any one model dominates every criterion.

| Architecture | Capability concentration | Researcher agenda control | Reproducibility | Speed | Agenda plurality |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Proprietary laboratory research | Very high | Low outside the laboratory | Low at generator level | Very high | Potentially low |
| Vendor-subsidized academic access | High | Substantially higher | Partial | High | Higher |
| Public-private research resource | Medium | High | Potentially high | Medium | High |
| Public or sovereign compute commons | Lower institutional concentration | High | Potentially high | Potentially lower | Potentially very high |

: Qualitative comparison of institutional architectures for frontier mathematical AI. No architecture simultaneously maximizes capability, decentralization, speed, and reproducibility. {#tbl-when-mathematics-became-a-repository-control-architectures}

The comparison also shows why open weights alone are insufficient. If reproducing the strongest research behaviour requires large inference budgets, then model access can be public while effective frontier cognition remains concentrated. This is why AGMAI's October statement explicitly coupled access to powerful AI tools with access to the computational resources needed to use them effectively.[^when-mathematics-became-a-repository-agmai-october]

The reverse is equally important. Public compute without sufficiently capable models or the surrounding orchestration stack does not reproduce the research system either. Effective capability depends on the model, the available compute, and the research harness around them: retrieval, proof assistants, agentic workflows, search procedures, formal environments, and evaluation infrastructure.

Allocation rules therefore matter as much as nominal access. Even a public compute commons must decide which researchers receive resources. Peer-reviewed merit, lotteries among qualified proposals, disciplinary quotas, support for early-career researchers, dedicated high-risk allocations, and reproducibility grants would all produce different mathematical frontiers.

No allocation rule is neutral because every rule embodies a value function.

A mathematically healthy infrastructure may therefore need to reserve part of its resources for exploration rather than optimizing entirely for near-term theorem yield. Famous open problems are attractive because success is legible. Eccentric definitions, speculative analogies, and low-probability research programmes are harder to evaluate but historically indispensable. Distributed access has epistemic value precisely because different mathematicians spend research capacity according to different tastes.

The same principle applies to verification and archival custody. Ideally, the institution allocating frontier machine cognition should not also be the sole verifier and permanent archive of its outputs. Generation, verification, and custody can be institutionally separated. A laboratory can generate the result, an independent formal system or mathematical organization can verify specific claims, and an independent scholarly repository can preserve the version history.

This is the organizational analogue of Comparator. Reliability does not require the generator to become universally trusted. It requires reducing how much must be trusted in any one actor.

Repository independence therefore matters for more than preservation. If the producing laboratory hosts the only authoritative copy of the mathematics, it controls the visible revision history, metadata, citation target, and presentation of corrections. An independent archive creates durable custody of what was claimed, when, and with which evidence.

The long-run target should consequently not be one universally trusted mathematical AI. It should be **plural infrastructure**: multiple capable models, multiple compute providers, independent proof checkers, independent archives, portable formal artifacts, and communities with different mathematical tastes.

The objective is not decentralization as an end in itself. It is reduction of correlated epistemic failure.

Interoperability may ultimately matter more than ownership. A conjecture formulated with one system should be inspectable by another. A proof generated by one laboratory should be independently checkable elsewhere. A theorem's dependency graph should not exist only inside one proprietary service. The mathematical object should retain identity when moved between repositories.

The production process can remain partly proprietary while the resulting mathematics remains epistemically portable.

That requirement also changes what mathematical institutions themselves must provide. Universities, institutes, societies, and funding agencies cannot demand distributed agency without building alternative infrastructure for model access, compute allocation, formal verification, archival preservation, young-researcher access, and priority resolution.

Agency requires institutions capable of exercising it.

Pure mathematics may therefore become more infrastructure-intensive than it has historically been. A future mathematics institute may need not only offices, libraries, and seminar rooms but guaranteed inference allocations, shared research agents, proof-assistant infrastructure, permanent repositories, and specialists in mathematical knowledge engineering.

The robust architecture is not one sovereign machine intelligence. It is a **federated epistemic system** in which different institutions control the functions for which they have legitimate competence.

## From papers to mathematical infrastructure

The argument can now return to the apparently mundane fact that initiated it: OpenAI released the corpus as a repository.

The reason this matters is not that mathematics should migrate from journals to GitHub. It is that the object being published had already acquired properties for which the paper is an incomplete container.

The conventional mathematical paper is an extraordinarily successful compression format. It states the theorem, establishes priority, contains the proof, cites dependencies, explains significance, records authorship, and provides a citable object. For most of mathematical history, these components changed slowly enough that one document could represent them together.

Machine-generated mathematics weakens that coincidence. The informal exposition may be revised after the proof is formalized. A Lean artifact may arrive after the paper. Independent review may strengthen or weaken confidence without altering the text. A later proof may be simpler. Dependencies may be discovered subsequently. Human understanding may mature years after the initial release.

The theorem should therefore acquire an identity independent of any one manuscript.

A more robust infrastructure would assign a persistent identifier to a mathematical claim and attach multiple artifacts to it: the informal statement, formal statement, proof objects, manuscripts, verification records, dependency information, expositions, revision history, and known consequences.

The paper would no longer be the sole scholarly object. It would become one representation of a richer one.

This also implies **semantic versioning for claims**. A textual diff can tell us that two source files differ. Mathematical infrastructure should additionally know whether a revision strengthened the conclusion, added a hypothesis, repaired a proof without changing the statement, corrected an attribution, or modified exposition only.

These are different epistemic events because their downstream consequences differ.

Formal statements provide a natural machine-readable anchor. If several papers, proofs, and explanations refer to the same formal theorem, the formal object can help establish theorem identity independently of textual similarity. This makes new queries possible: which papers prove exactly this statement; which results depend on it; which formal proofs invoke a given axiom; which manuscript makes a stronger natural-language claim than its associated formal theorem?

But the semantic bridge between the informal theorem and the formal statement must itself be represented. A Boolean such as `formalized: true` is inadequate. The repository should distinguish the existence of a formal statement, existence of a proof, kernel acceptance, permitted axioms, Comparator or equivalent target checking, and the status of independent review of the informal/formal correspondence.

Provenance should become a graph rather than an author field. The relevant lineage may include the original conjecture, earlier literature, problem selection, model invocation, candidate proof, formalization, computational certificate, human edits, independent review, and later exposition. These are different relations and should be typed accordingly.

The same applies to citations. A paper may cite another because it depends on a theorem, borrows terminology, gives historical credit, compares approaches, or generalizes an idea. Machine reasoning over the literature requires typed edges rather than generic bibliographic links.

Once these relations are machine-readable, continuous integration has a mathematical analogue. A change to an upstream theorem or definition can trigger formal rebuilds, dependency checks, axiom audits, and impact analysis. For formal mathematics, this is not metaphorical. If a dependency changes, downstream proofs can be rerun automatically.

The literature then begins to behave less like a shelf and more like a maintained system.

Dependency information can also inform research itself. A theorem supporting many conditional consequences may have unusually high downstream leverage. That should never become a universal measure of importance—high centrality can reflect fashion, and low-centrality questions can create entirely new fields—but it is one machine-readable signal that can contribute to research triage.

Explanations also need multiple resolutions. A theorem may need a one-paragraph conceptual summary, a specialist proof sketch, a detailed human-readable paper, and a complete formal derivation. These are not redundant versions of the same object. They optimize for different epistemic functions: conceptual compression, expert reconstruction, contextual argument, and logical assurance.

Methods deserve persistent identity as well. If several theorems use the same new construction, the durable contribution may be the method rather than the individual proof. A method object could record its conceptual description, minimal hypotheses, canonical examples, formal lemmas, applications, and known limitations.

Open problems should likewise become first-class objects. Their state could include the canonical statement, equivalent formulations, origin and attribution, partial results, failed approaches, conditional consequences, candidate solutions, formalization state, and current review status. This becomes particularly useful once several AI systems can attack the same frontier simultaneously.

The result is a mathematical literature with an API in the epistemic rather than merely software sense. Research agents could query exact statements, dependencies, proof status, versions, explanations, and methods instead of treating papers only as opaque text documents.

The paper remains indispensable in this architecture. Its role changes.

Rather than being the sole container of evidence, it becomes the principal human explanatory layer: the place where the reader learns why the theorem matters, where the obstruction lay, what idea resolved it, and what should be remembered. Result abundance makes such narrative more valuable because conceptual compression becomes scarcer.

Scholarly publication may likewise evolve from certifying one frozen document toward certifying properties of a living mathematical object. Formal correctness, semantic fidelity, novelty, attribution, exposition, and significance need not be judged by the same actor or at the same time.

Persistent identity then becomes crucial. Repository paths change, commercial platforms disappear, and titles evolve. A mathematical claim should remain citable across migrations. AGMAI's recommendation for independent scholarly repositories with persistent identifiers and preserved histories is therefore more than archival hygiene; it is a requirement for maintaining scholarly identity under versioned publication.[^when-mathematics-became-a-repository-agmai-recommendations]

Custody and computation should remain separable as well. The laboratory supplying the strongest model need not also be the permanent custodian of the theorem. Independent archives and independent verification systems allow the mathematical object to survive changes in commercial strategy, model generation, or institutional power.

The repository then becomes an external memory system for research agents. Model weights are poor custodians of exact, evolving scholarly state. A maintained repository can record which theorem version is current, which proof is checked, which assumptions are active, which downstream results depend on it, and which explanations have appeared.

This creates a recursive research architecture: machine-readable literature informs AI research; AI research generates new candidate results; formal and human verification update their status; the repository changes; the revised corpus becomes the input to the next research cycle.

That is much stronger than using a language model to answer isolated mathematical questions.

It also introduces new failure modes. Incorrect metadata can propagate automatically. A mistaken mapping between informal and formal statements can contaminate downstream dependencies. Significance scores can create self-reinforcing fashions. Repository schemas may privilege mathematics that formalizes cleanly. Central APIs can become new control points.

The knowledge graph must therefore not be confused with mathematics itself.

Research taste, analogy, heuristic reasoning, geometric intuition, and tacit understanding will remain difficult to encode completely. The infrastructure should extend mathematical culture, not attempt to replace it with nodes and edges.

The likely future is hybrid: formal proof objects, machine-readable metadata, versioned repositories, human-readable papers, seminars, workshops, interactive explanations, surveys, and textbooks. Each medium serves a different epistemic function.

GitHub is therefore evidence, not the endpoint. Its significance lies in supplying enough repository primitives to expose the inadequacy of a static PDF archive for this new kind of output. A mature infrastructure will need properties GitHub does not natively provide: theorem-level persistent identity, typed epistemic state, formal/informal correspondence records, mathematical dependency graphs, independent certification, priority records, durable archival governance, and machine-readable method objects.

The durable transition is not from journals to GitHub.

It is from **the paper as the sole primary epistemic object to a maintained mathematical knowledge object**.

## Conclusion: after the paper

On 6 October 2026, OpenAI released 722 manuscripts organized into 372 result families spanning seventeen areas of mathematics and theoretical computer science. The collection emerged from approximately 4,000 posed research problems and included not only natural-language papers but formalizations, Comparator artifacts, reasoning summaries, computational material, provenance, citation guidance, and explicit version history.[^when-mathematics-became-a-repository-openai-release]

The conspicuous fact was the mathematics.

The more revealing fact may have been the form of publication.

The event belongs to a broader sequence. Proof generation becomes cheaper, so verification becomes relatively more valuable. Formal proof systems make parts of verification scalable. Repeated research-level successes produce result abundance. Result abundance creates an epistemic backlog between what has been generated and what has been understood. Mathematical digestion—validation, conceptual compression, method extraction, contextualization, and canonicalization—becomes a research activity in its own right. When thousands of problems can receive machine effort, attention and eventually mathematical agency become scarce.

The most important new category is therefore not false mathematics but **unmetabolized mathematics**: results that may be correct, formally certified, and important while remaining incompletely understood or integrated into the working structure of a field.

This distinction also explains why the October corpus remains significant even after aggressive qualification. The release does not demonstrate a 9.3 percent success rate on arbitrary open problems. It does not establish that all 372 families are correct. It does not show that an autonomous AI mathematician independently selected the research programme. Those stronger claims are unsupported by the public evidence.

A narrower statement is sufficient: **frontier mathematical discovery has become a repeatable output of a computational research process**.

The significance of that statement grows because mathematics is a dependency network. A high-leverage theorem can alter the status of many downstream results. The scientific value of a machine research system is therefore not captured by paper count. It depends on where its results sit in the mathematical graph, whether the proofs survive scrutiny, whether novel methods emerge, and whether the community can assimilate them.

The final scarcity consequently moves upstream. If powerful models can attack many important questions in parallel, then choosing which questions deserve that capability becomes an allocation decision with scientific consequences. Mathematical agency becomes part of the infrastructure problem.

That is why the governance debate is inseparable from the mathematics. Control of frontier models, compute, and problem selection can determine where machine cognition is deployed before any paper is written. Public release restores access to the result, but not necessarily equality of opportunity in discovery.

The appropriate long-run architecture is therefore unlikely to be either one proprietary mathematical laboratory or one universally open model. A more resilient system would combine capable private and public research systems, broad researcher access, shared compute, independent verification, independent archives, portable formal artifacts, and plural agenda setting.

Authorship will evolve for the same reason. Contribution, understanding, verification, exposition, and responsibility can now belong to different actors. Provenance needs to become richer, while accountability must remain attached to humans and institutions capable of exercising judgment.

The paper survives this transformation. Indeed, it becomes more important as result abundance increases, because human readers need explanation and conceptual compression more than ever. What changes is the paper's job.

A future mathematical result will increasingly be represented by a larger package: a human-readable theorem, a formal counterpart where available, one or more proofs, machine-checkable certificates, dependency and provenance information, explanatory layers, and an explicit version and review state. The paper is the layer optimized for understanding; the repository preserves the state required for reliable cumulative use.

The strongest interpretation of the October release is therefore not that mathematics has become software, that GitHub should replace journals, or that repository commits confer truth.

It is that the scholarly object is becoming **maintained rather than merely published**.

The proof may change. The exposition may improve. A formalization may arrive later. Dependencies may be added. Verification may strengthen. Attribution may be corrected. Human understanding may deepen.

The theorem's truth is not versioned. The epistemic object surrounding it is.

That is what *repository mathematics* means: a regime in which mathematical knowledge must be continuously represented, verified, linked, interpreted, and governed because its machine-generated production rate has begun to rise.

The repository is therefore not merely where the mathematics is stored. It becomes part of the machinery by which mathematics continues.

The decisive question after proof abundance is no longer simply whether an AI can prove a theorem.

It is what happens when AI systems can continuously produce part of the mathematical frontier, while humans, machines, and institutions jointly decide which results become knowledge.
